Recall where this enzyme must start working in PCR - it cannot start on bare single-stranded DNA, it needs a short double-stranded starting point.
Focus on the temperatures in the PCR cycle - denaturation is at about $95 ^\circ\text{C}$ and extension at about $72 ^\circ\text{C}$. What problem would a normal human enzyme face here?
Link that heat stability to why PCR can run for 30+ cycles automatically without adding fresh enzyme each time.
walkthrough:
What Taq Does - Build DNA**
Taq polymerase is the DNA polymerase used in PCR. Its job is to synthesise a new complementary DNA strand using the separated target strand as a template.

How It Starts - Needs A Primer**
It binds to the annealed primers and then adds free DNA nucleotides to the 3-prime end of the primer. This happens in the extension stage, joining adjacent nucleotides with phosphodiester bonds.

Why Taq Is Special - Heat Stability**
PCR repeatedly heats DNA to about $95 ^\circ\text{C}$ to separate strands. Normal enzymes would denature and lose shape at this temperature. Taq has an optimum around $72 ^\circ\text{C}$ and is thermostable, so it stays folded and active at $95 ^\circ\text{C}$.

Why That Matters - Repeated Cycles**
Because it survives denaturation, Taq does not need replacing each cycle. The same enzyme can catalyse synthesis through many cycles, allowing exponential amplification.

Final answer: Taq polymerase is a thermostable DNA polymerase. It binds to primers on target DNA and synthesises a complementary new DNA strand by adding DNA nucleotides during extension at about $72 ^\circ\text{C}$, forming phosphodiester bonds. It does not denature at $95 ^\circ\text{C}$ so is not used up and can be used for many PCR cycles.

walkthrough:
Link Length To Position**
You are told normal product is longer than mutant product. In Fig. 3.1 the direction of DNA movement is downwards, so bands nearer the top are longer and bands further down are shorter.

Read The Children**
Child 1 shows only the upper long band, so only normal allele. Child 2 shows only the lower short band, so mutant allele. Child 3 shows both bands, so carries the mutant allele as well. Both child 2 and child 3 have the mutation and cannot safely receive gentamicin.
Final answer: Child 2 and child 3 (both show the shorter, further-moved mutant allele band).

walkthrough:
Why DNA Moves**
The phosphate groups make every DNA fragment negatively charged. When voltage is applied, fragments are pulled from the negative cathode toward the positive anode, which is downwards in Fig. 3.1.

How Size Creates The Pattern**
The agarose gel acts like a mesh. All fragments have the same charge per unit length, so separation is by size only. Smaller fragments slip through pores easily and migrate faster and further in the same time. Larger fragments are held back and stay closer to the wells.

Apply To Normal And Mutant Alleles**
The normal MT-RNR1 PCR product is longer, so it moves slowly and forms the upper band seen in child 1. The mutant product is shorter, so it moves faster and further to form the lower band seen in child 2.

Explain All Three Lanes**
Child 1 is homozygous normal, so one upper band only. Child 2 shows only the lower mutant band. Child 3 shows both an upper and a lower band because both length variants are present in that sample, giving two bands in one lane.

Final answer: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size/length. DNA is negatively charged so moves toward the anode. Smaller/shorter fragments migrate faster and further through the gel. The longer normal MT-RNR1 product travels a shorter distance (upper band) and the shorter mutant product travels further (lower band).

hints: This is movement of a gene between living bacteria of the same generation, not parent to offspring - think of the name for direct plasmid sharing between cells.
walkthrough:
Plasmids Move Sideways**
Resistance genes on plasmids can pass from one bacterium to another in the same generation. This is horizontal transmission. The most common route is conjugation, where a donor cell passes a copy of the plasmid directly to a recipient through a pilus. Transduction by bacteriophage or transformation by uptake of free DNA are also valid routes.
Final answer: Horizontal transmission by conjugation / transfer of plasmids between bacteria (accept transduction, transformation, transfection).
